To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the surficial deposits of the North-Central Lake Superior region are complex, and the glacial events that produced them are also complex.

the surficial glacial geology of the area indicates that the area was covered by a complex series of stationary ice fronts, glacial lakes and readvances during deglaciation, and that the Nakina Moraine was built 9 400 to 9 200 years ago, and the last ice disappeared from the area about 6 390 to 6 300 years ago.
a complex history of ice fronts and glaciolakustre lakes is recorded by surficial glacial deposits in a region of northern Ontario.
In summary, our research is concerned with

reconstructing the glacial history of the north-central part of Lake Superior, an area of 13 000 sq. miles, in the vicinity of the Nakina morainic complex, which extends from Lake Superior to Lake Nipigon.
the deglaciation of the Lake Superior and adjacent areas.
the reconstruction of the history of the last ice age in the Lake Superior region, with special emphasis on the glacial and post-glacial lakes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the glacial history of this area is complex, with a number of glacial advances and retreats.
the area has a history of at least three major glacial advances and at least two major glacial lakes, and that the area has been ice-free for at least 6 390 radiocarbon years.
this part of the Lake Superior region was deglaciated by 9 000 years ago.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(1) The Lake Superior basin was occupied by a series of glacial lakes, and the northern part of the area by Lake Nakina, which was later overridden by readvances of the Superior lobe; (2) The Superior lobe was the last to disappear from the area.

the Lake Nipigion basin was filled to 500 feet by a glacial lake at the close of the Minong glaciation, that this lake was drained through a spillway near Lake Superior, that the Superior basin was filled by glacial lake waters to at least 400 feet, and that a glacial lake 300 feet deep occupied the Lake Nakina basin.
the glacial history of the area is complex and not easily interpreted, and that the ice was not as thick as is generally supposed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the last glacial advance was not the most recent advance to reach our area.
there is no need to invoke an ice-dammed lake to explain the origin of Lake Superior.
the ice sheet was not a simple entity.
